sources.title: W. B. Hafford: Archaeology in the Digital Age, the ancient city of Ur
sources.note: Penn Museum, 2013, directly opened. Introductory site history places Ur near Nasiriyah in southern Iraq, occupied approximately 5000 to 500 BCE, and links abandonment to movement of the Euphrates. Earlier habitation is not treated as a securely dated urban founding. Biblical Abraham identification excluded.

sources.title: Lee Horne: Ur and Its Treasures, the Royal Tombs
sources.note: Penn Museum, 1998, direct/indexed original article. Ur and the Royal Cemetery section: waterway access to Gulf, urban growth during third millennium, Nanna, and circa 1850 excavated burials mostly simple. Broad gold supply discussion is about likely regions, not provenance certification for a particular object. Older absolute founding/occupation generalizations not used.

sources.title: Metropolitan Museum of Art: Ur, the Ziggurat
sources.note: Direct museum essay, 2002. Around 2100 BCE Ur-Nammu control over southern cities and temple building; lost upper stages versus reconstructed design and modern restoration of lower stages. Does not claim ziggurat was a tomb or Ur invented stepped temples.

sources.title: Richard L. Zettler: From Beneath the Temple, Inscribed Objects from Ur
sources.note: Direct Penn Museum scholarly article, 1986. Context: Ur III 2112 to 2004 BCE, Nimintabba temple. Brick boxes beneath northeastern wall held basket-bearing peg figures and steatite tablets; inscriptions identify Shulgi and building. Pooled with existing Sumer card use. Speculative functions of bone-filled cylinders not presented as certain.

sources.title: Electronic Text Corpus of Sumerian Royal Inscriptions: Ur-Namma 19
sources.note: Original indexed scholarly composite, RIME 3/2.01.01.19, cones from Ur, Ur III. Column i 1 to ii 6 royal claim to drain swamp planted with date palms and construct levee; ii 7 to 8 gives name. Numbers and converted area omitted. Royal claim distinguished from a measured excavation of the drainage system.

sources.title: British Museum: Standard of Ur, museum number 121201
sources.note: Direct/indexed official catalogue. Early Dynastic III, 2550 to 2400 BCE, PG 779, shell/red limestone/lapis mosaics, banquet with singer and lyre player, reconstructed box-like form and unknown original purpose. No claim this depicts all households or a certain military flag.

sources.title: British Museum: Puabi’s lapis lazuli seal, museum number 121544
sources.note: Official catalogue, indexed complete record. Mid-third-millennium royal cemetery object, U.10939, inscription and banquet scenes. BM date 2600 BCE differs from CDLI period label ED IIIb 2500 to 2340 BCE; public gives broad mid-third-millennium dating. Not confused with Penn B16728, a different seal whose entry discusses this one.

sources.title: Cuneiform Digital Library Initiative: Puabi seal, P247683
sources.note: Direct full artifact record: BM121544, U10939, PG800; lines 1 pu3-ad, 2 nin; English Pu-abum / the queen. Public uses scholarly Roman-letter transliteration pu₃-ad / nin, explicitly not original wedge glyphs. Conventional Puabi name from museum is distinguished from CDLI translation Pu-abum. No Unicode sign rendering invented.

sources.title: C. Leonard Woolley: Excavations at Ur, 1930 to 1931
sources.note: Direct original excavation report, 1931, Larsa house quarter, No. III Straight Street, rooms 2, 3, 5, 9. Modern street names were assigned by excavators. Old absolute chronology is obsolete and not reused; date early second millennium follows modern Penn scholarship. Paved rooms interpreted as lavatory/washing room are explicitly excavator interpretations. No modern flushing, sewer-network or health guarantee.

sources.title: Steve Tinney: Texts, Tablets, and Teaching
sources.note: Direct Penn Museum scholarly article. Archaeology of schooling section, No. 7 Quiet Street: over 2000 texts, dateable pieces first half of eighteenth century BCE, possible paired dictation exercises. Shared URL with Sumer card; cumulative budget checked. No universal schooling, imagined student age, or assertion that all 2000 are homework.

sources.title: British Museum: Nanni’s letter to Ea-nasir, museum number 131236
sources.note: Official full indexed catalogue: Old Babylonian, around 1750 BCE, Ur provenance, copper quality complaint after Gulf voyage and misdirection/delay. No world-first complaint claim, meme embellishment, unsourced exact quotations or house attribution.

sources.title: Enrica Inversi: Music for children, a fired clay rattle from Ur
sources.note: British Museum Middle East Newsletter 8 (2023), printed page 40. Full indexed original page text checked; direct PDF fails. Pig-shaped hollow body, clay balls, 1923/24 excavation; broad type most common Isin-Larsa. Interpretation as toy, musical or protective object retained. Most Digdiggah surface finds have uncertain context; do not assign this pig to an identified nursery or exact household.

sources.title: William B. Hafford: City of the Moon, New Excavations at Ur
sources.note: Direct Penn Museum field report, 2017. 2015 AH Niche Lane Trench 2 balance-pan weights and economic texts; modern dating distinction between Old Babylonian homes and Ur III reused bricks. Used also as chronological support for house section. Pooled with existing Sumer card. No uncertain mother/child figurine dates silently moved into map span.

sources.title: Elizabeth Knott: The Isin-Larsa and Old Babylonian Periods
sources.note: Direct museum essay revised 2025. Opening chronology, collapse of Ur III around 2004 BCE; Isin controlled Ur and Nippur, followed by Larsa/Babylon predominance. No claim Ur city ended with its dynasty; no conflation of regional epoch endpoints and city destruction.

sources.title: Royal Inscriptions of Babylonia Online: Nabonidus 32
sources.note: Full indexed original edition, Nabonidus 32, Ur cylinders including BM91128 and BM91125. Column i 5 to 21: older Ur-Namma/Shulgi inscriptions, incomplete/completed ziggurat, repair with bitumen and baked brick. Explicitly sixth-century BCE later history. Direct Oracc fetch unreliable.

sources.title: British Museum: Nabonidus cylinder from Ur, museum number 91128
sources.note: Full indexed official catalogue: sixth-century BCE object, dated 555 to 539 BCE, Ur provenance and temple-restoration text. Provides dated physical witness for RIBo edition. Older finder metadata is not used.

proposedOverrides.summary: Ur was a long-lived city in southern Mesopotamia and the capital of the much shorter Third Dynasty of Ur.

batchIdentityNotes.finding: Exact indexed Ur, imported -4000 to-1500, previously no runtime card or override. All matching border snapshots decoded in identities.json: enormous repeated bbox about40.81 to50.13E/29.27to35.72N. Not a reliable city/state boundary; overview explicitly rejects continuous regional control. Narrative distinguishes archaeological site and city, Early Dynastic elite cemetery, short Ur III imperial phase2112to2004BCE, later Old Babylonian households, and sixth-centuryBCE repairs outside map. No alias with Sumer, Uruk or other cities. Existing Sumer card remains; shared sources counted cumulatively. No fell/successors override or invented map extension.
